modern:
To the gods I owe it that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, good relatives and friends, nearly everything good. Further, I owe it to the gods that I was not hurried into any offence against any of them, though I had a disposition which, had the opportunity arisen, might have led me to do something of the kind; but, through their favour, circumstances never came together to put me to the test. Further, I am thankful to the gods that I was not brought up any longer with my grandfather’s mistress, and that I kept the flower of my youth, and that I did not prove my manhood before the proper time, but even put it off; that I was placed under a ruler and father who was able to take all pride away from me, and to bring me to understand that it is possible for a man to live in a palace without needing guards or embroidered clothes, or torches and statues, and such-like show; but that it is in such a man’s power to bring himself very close to the way of life of a private citizen, without being for this reason either meaner in thought or more careless in action with respect to the things which must be done for the public interest in a way that befits a ruler. I thank the gods for giving me such a brother, who was able by his moral character to rouse me to watchfulness over myself, and who at the same time pleased me by his respect and affection; that my children have not been stupid or deformed in body; that I did not make more progress in rhetoric, poetry, and the other studies, in which I might perhaps have become completely absorbed if I had seen that I was making progress in them; that I made haste to give those who brought me up the positions of honour which they seemed to want, without putting them off with the hope that I would do it some other time, since they were then still young; that I knew Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus; that I received clear and frequent impressions about living according to nature, and what kind of life that is, so that, as far as it depended on the gods, and their gifts, and help, and inspirations, nothing prevented me from living according to nature straight away, though I still fall short of it through my own fault, and through not heeding the warnings of the gods and, I might almost say, their direct instructions; that my body has held out so long in such a way of life; that I never touched either Benedicta or Theodotus, and that, after falling into passionate love, I was cured; and, though I was often out of humour with Rusticus, I never did anything I had cause to regret; that, though it was my mother’s fate to die young, she spent the last years of her life with me; that, whenever I wished to help anyone in need, or on any other occasion, I was never told that I did not have the means to do it; and that I myself never had the same need, to receive anything from another; that I have such a wife, so obedient, so affectionate, and so simple; that I had plenty of good teachers for my children; and that remedies have been shown to me in dreams, among others against spitting blood and dizziness...; and that, when I became inclined to philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of any sophist, and that I did not waste my time on writers of histories, or on solving syllogisms, or busy myself investigating appearances in the heavens; for all these things require the help of the gods and of fortune.

Among the Quadi, at the Granua.
original:
To the gods I am indebted for having good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good associates, good kinsmen and friends, nearly everything good. Further, I owe it to the gods that I was not hurried into any offence against any of them, though I had a disposition which, if opportunity had offered, might have led me to do something of this kind; but, through their favor, there never was such a concurrence of circumstances as put me to the trial. Further, I am thankful to the gods that I was not longer brought up with my grandfather’s concubine, and that I preserved the flower of my youth, and that I did not make proof of my virility before the proper season, but even deferred the time; that I was subjected to a ruler and father who was able to take away all pride from me, and to bring me to the knowledge that it is possible for a man to live in a palace without wanting either guards or embroidered dresses, or torches and statues, and such-like show; but that it is in such a man’s power to bring himself very near to the fashion of a private person, without being for this reason either meaner in thought, or more remiss in action, with respect to the things which must be done for the public interest in a manner that befits a ruler. I thank the gods for giving me such a brother, who was able by his moral character to rouse me to vigilance over myself, and who at the same time pleased me by his respect and affection; that my children have not been stupid nor deformed in body; that I did not make more proficiency in rhetoric, poetry, and the other studies, in which I should perhaps have been completely engaged, if I had seen that I was making progress in them; that I made haste to place those who brought me up in the station of honor, which they seemed to desire, without putting them off with hope of my doing it some other time after, because they were then still young; that I knew Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus; that I received clear and frequent impressions about living according to nature, and what kind of a life that is, so that, so far as depended on the gods, and their gifts, and help, and inspirations, nothing hindered me from forthwith living according to nature, though I still fall short of it through my own fault, and through not observing the admonitions of the gods, and, I may almost say, their direct instructions; that my body has held out so long in such a kind of life; that I never touched either Benedicta or Theodotus, and that, after having fallen into amatory passions, I was cured, and, though I was often out of humor with Rusticus, I never did anything of which I had occasion to repent; that, though it was my mother’s fate to die young, she spent the last years of her life with me; that, whenever I wished to help any man in his need, or on any other occasion, I was never told that I had not the means of doing it; and that to myself the same necessity never happened, to receive anything from another; that I have such a wife, so obedient, and so affectionate, and so simple; that I had abundance of good masters for my children; and that remedies have been shown to me by dreams, both others, and against bloodspitting and giddiness...; and that, when I had an inclination to philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of any sophist, and that I did not waste my time on writers [of histories], or in the resolution of syllogisms, or occupy myself about the investigation of appearances in the heavens; for all these things require the help of the gods and fortune.

Among the Quadi at the Granua.
